Chapter Twenty-two: The Tathāgata (end of section nine). Chapter Twenty-two: The Tathāgata.
There are generally two gates to Mahayana contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). The twenty-one preceding chapters sought the persons and dharmas of the mundane world.
One cannot attain clarity regarding the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) of the Mahāyāna.
From this point downward, the four chapters seek the dharma of those who have left the world; since it cannot be attained, one cannot fully discern the Mahāyāna contemplative practice.
The dharmas of worldly people are coarse and easy to observe.
Therefore, I clarify this first.
The supramundane dharmas of the Buddhas are subtle and difficult to refute;
for this reason, they are explained later.
Furthermore, from the preceding section onwards, the opponent has attempted to rescue the world by appealing to worldly conventions;
since that argument failed to establish its point,
this present chapter rescues the world by appealing to the supramundane.
Since there is a supramundane, there must be a mundane.
Therefore, the Master [Vasubandhu] first refutes the supramundane;
once the supramundane does not exist, how could the mundane exist?
Furthermore, both those of the Great Vehicle and those of the Small Vehicle say that there are two: the mundane and the supramundane.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The wise and ignorance—fools call these two."
The wise fully comprehend that these are non-dual.
Now, I wish to demonstrate that there are no two distinct characteristics between the mundane and the supramundane;
since they are non-dual, [there is no difference].
Furthermore, there is neither non-duality, nor both duality and non-duality, nor that which is neither dual nor non-dual.
One thus enters into the true nature of reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and gives rise to right contemplation (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), whereby conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is extinguished.
Therefore, one next contemplates that which transcends the world (*lokottara*).

Furthermore, those who are deluded perceive the duality of the mundane and the supramundane; thus, both the mundane and the supramundane together constitute the world, and they are unable to transcend the world.
Now, when one thoroughly realizes that the mundane and the supramundane are non-dual, this is truly termed "supramundane."
In order to lead outsiders to realize the supramundane by means of the mundane, he refutes the supramundane.
This chapter consists of four sections in total.
The first is the refutation of the Tathāgata.
Second, it subverts the perversions;
third, it subverts the Four Noble Truths;
fourth, it subverts nirvana.
The refutation of the mundane is extensive,
consisting of twenty-one chapters;
the refutation of the supramundane is concise.
The reason for clarifying only these four categories is to demonstrate the mutual manifestation of the detailed and the concise;
furthermore, it reveals that even what is grasped as supramundane is still mundane.
Since the mundane has already been refuted above.
This concludes the refutation of the supramundane;
therefore, there is no need for an extensive refutation.
Furthermore, the mundane is the basis for the supramundane.
Since the root has already declined, the branches are easily broken;
therefore, there are only four categories.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is the supreme person who has transcended the world.
Nirvāṇa is the supreme, ultimate dharma.
This refers to the pair of person and phenomena.
"Perversion" refers to the false delusions that are to be destroyed.
The Four Noble Truths are the orthodox teaching capable of destroying [delusion].
That is to say, they constitute the pair of the false and the correct;
briefly elucidating them through four gates, there is no principle that is not encompassed.
Furthermore, to destroy the Tathāgata is to destroy the person;
from the three lower categories downward, it is to destroy the dharmas.
Although there are many things that transcend the world, they do not go beyond the person and the dharmas.
In sum, all things are subsumed;
the mundane world is likewise,
for it does not transcend persons and phenomena.
This summarizes everything.
It is divided into two parts:
the chapter "Contemplating the Tathāgata" clarifies the transcendence of the emptiness of persons.
The next three chapters clarify the emptiness of supramundane phenomena.
Previously, within the mundane section, they were simply divided into two categories based on their breadth and brevity;
now, they are distinguished by way of persons and phenomena.
As for persons, there is only one category; since a person cannot be manifold, they are not two.
However, dharmas have many gates.
Furthermore, while the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is easy to realize, the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is difficult to clarify.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence of the four categories: since there have been Buddhas appearing in the world in the past, one first contemplates the Tathāgata.
The reason the Tathāgata appears in the world is to destroy the afflictions of sentient beings.
Therefore, next one contemplates the perversions (*viparyāsa*).
Since the perversions are overcome by means of the teaching of the Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*),
one next contemplates the Four Noble Truths.
Although the Four Noble Truths are taught, their ultimate purpose converges upon a single cessation;
therefore, Nirvana is explained last.
Possessing these four gateways, it encompasses all meanings.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata is one who has transcended the world;
inversion is that which the Tathāgata has abandoned;
and the Four Noble Truths are that which the Tathāgata contemplates.
Nirvana is that which is realized by the Tathāgata;
it is furthermore a sequential path.
Moreover, the previous refutation of the Tathāgata demonstrated the mutual manifestation of the mundane and the supramundane.
In worldly dharmas, one first refutes the doctrine and subsequently refutes the person;
in supramundane dharmas, one first examines the person and subsequently refutes the doctrine.
Thus say those of the two external schools.
The Tathāgata is able to expound both mundane and supramundane dharmas.
Since there is one who is able to expound them,
there must necessarily be the dharmas that are expounded.
Regarding the third point, "arising from the categories of formation and destruction":
the world is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing; thus, it can be said that it is non-existent [in its ultimate nature].
The Tathāgata is a dharma that is neither born nor extinguished;
he must therefore exist. Furthermore, internally he has destroyed the thieves of the fetters, and externally he has shattered the armies of Māra.
Since there is a Tathāgata, there is consequently arising and ceasing.
Fourth, the final verse of the superior grade states:
"One seeks the three realms of existence but does not find them."
The opponent says:
If one is free from the three realms of existence, that is the Tathāgata;
therefore, there must be a Buddha.
That which is called the "Tathāgata" is the most essential point among all the meanings in this chapter.

Now, whether followers of the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, they set their intent upon believing in the Buddha, recollecting the Buddha, prostrating to the Buddha, taking refuge in the Buddha, becoming disciples of the Buddha, and seeking the path of the Buddha.
If one recognizes the Buddha, all matters and purposes will be accomplished;
if one does not recognize the Buddha and does not seek the Buddha, all matters will be ruined.
Therefore, one must recognize the Buddha with diligence.
In terms of the Dharma, his essence comes as it truly is;
therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
In terms of persons, he comes like all Buddhas; thus he is named the Tathāgata.
Regarding the explanation of the term based on its transformation of sentient beings: it is called "Tathāgata" because [the Buddha] comes in response to those who perceive him.
Thus, various interpretations of "Tathāgata" are explained.
First, the non-Buddhists;
second, the Hīnayāna;
third, the Vaipulya.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) postulate a real self, which they call the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"I have various names, such as Manuṣya, Deva, and Tathāgata."
There are briefly three explanations regarding the Hīnayāna.
First, the Vātsīputrīya school says:
"The harmonious conjunction of the five pure aggregates constitutes a distinct person and dharma, which is called the Tathāgata."
The masters of the *Tattvasiddhi* clarify that the person who is provisionally designated is the essence of the Tathāgata;
or they say that, although provisional, there exists a distinct substance, function, and name.
Some say that [the Tathāgata] has neither substance nor function;
others say that he has no substance but possesses function.
Thirdly, the Abhidharma explains two kinds of Tathāgatas.
First, the five aggregates with outflows constitute the birth-body Tathāgata;
second, the five aggregates without outflows constitute the Dharma-body Buddha.
Therefore, [the Bodhisattva] practices for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and cultivates the karma for the marks and signs for one hundred kalpas.
Afterwards, one attains Buddhahood through thirty-four moments of mind.
While abiding in untainted (anāsrava) states of mind, one is not bound by conditions;
upon emerging from tainted (sāsrava) states, one is then bound by conditions.
The masters of the Mahāyāna *Abhidharmakośa* school establish five periods of the Buddha’s teaching:
in the first period, he attains Buddhahood with a body composed of the five aggregates;
in the second period, he takes omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) as his Buddha-nature.
He shares the same lifespan as the Buddhas of the Initial Teaching, eighty years.
Zhaoti (Zhaocheng) says:
"The Second Period is especially venerable."
In the third period, he practiced for immeasurable kalpas;
in the fourth period as well, he practiced for many kalpas,
surpassing the sands of the Ganges in the past.
In the future, it will be double the number above;
this is clarified in the fifth period.
The Buddha is eternally abiding, and the Buddha has no form.
There is only a single perfect wisdom that possesses universal sovereignty;
therefore, it is called "Buddha.
If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, one should manifest in form.
Regarding the explanation of the fifth period, there are four masters in total.
One says: "The essence of the Tathāgata is subsumed within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)."
Second, the explanation:
Since it is stated that the Tathāgata is precisely True Suchness (tathatā) as the Buddha,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says:
As suchness is without coming or going, suchness itself is the Buddha.
Furthermore, according to the masters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* in the northern lands, the Buddha has three bodies;
the Dharma-body Buddha is precisely suchness.
The essence of true thusness (tathatā) is not itself the Buddha, yet because it can give birth to the Buddha,
it is called "Buddha.
The mark of reality (yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa) is not itself prajñā, yet because it can give birth to prajñā, it is called "prajñā."
The two bodies—the retributive and the transformational—are subsumed within the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
Therefore, although there are three bodies, they are subsumed within only the two truths. Thus it is said in [the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*]: "Four."
The numinous wisdom of the Buddha-fruit is not subsumed within the two truths.
Because its essence is not false or provisional, it is not the conventional truth;
yet it cannot be identified with emptiness, nor can it be distinct from true non-existence.
Therefore, the Dharmakāya transcends the two truths.
The "Earth Treatise" (Dilun) school’s doctrine of the non-real is no different from that of the Sāṃkhya school.
The "True Doctrine" (Zhenzong) school clarifies the three types of Buddha-nature.
Because the non-abiding path serves as the cause,
there is the sixteen-foot transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*).
Because the path of assistance serves as the cause, through the fulfillment of the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one attains the recompense Buddha (*vipākakāya-buddha*).
Realizing the Way serves as the cause for attaining the Dharma-Buddha;
yet, if one now seeks this Tathāgata, it is entirely unobtainable.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata."
Question: If one were to negate all Buddhas, there would be no Buddha at all.
Answer: The outsider conceives of the Buddha within the framework of the four propositions; therefore, he negates the Buddha.
Now, we negate such a Buddha as defined by these four propositions.
To cease the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of sentient beings is precisely what constitutes knowing the Buddha.
Furthermore, although those of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna hold differing views and disagree, they all ultimately maintain that there is a Buddha.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti rebuked Subhūti, saying:
"If, Subhūti, you do not see the Buddha and do not hear the Dharma, then you may take this food.
This clarifies that if Śāriputra (Śunakṣatra) perceives a Buddha to be seen and a Dharma to be heard,
he is said to have "attained something," and is thus unfit to receive the food.
If one is able to see no Buddha, that is truly seeing the Buddha;
if there is no Dharma to be heard, that is truly hearing the Dharma.
Only then is one fit to receive food.
Furthermore, those who grasp at attainment regard the Buddha as right view and non-Buddhists as wrong view;
thus, they give rise to the two views of the wrong and the right.
Therefore, Vimalakīrti rebuked them, saying:
"The six teachers are your teachers;
only then may you take this food.
This clarifies that if one perceives the heterodox and the orthodox as two, [one is not yet free].
Thus, the seven Buddhas would be unable to accept food from the six teachers.
However, if one realizes that the heterodox and the orthodox are non-dual in essence— that the six teachers are themselves the seven Buddhas—
then this present chapter precisely clarifies that sentient beings and the Buddha possess no two distinct characteristics.
Therefore, the following verse says:
"The nature possessed by the Tathāgata is itself the nature of the world;
one who can understand it in this way truly knows the Buddha."
Furthermore, the treatise refutes fourteen types of views regarding the Buddha,
namely the four permutations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The first is the calculation that the Buddha exists as a conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Second, calculating that the Buddha is the emptiness of ultimate truth;
third, calculating that the Buddha is comprised of both truths;
fourth, calculating that the Buddha is neither empty nor existent, transcending the two truths.
Next, the four lines [indicate that] the Hīnayāna maintains that the Buddha is impermanent,
while the Mahāyāna maintains that the Buddha is eternal;
when the three bodies (trikāya) are discussed together, he possesses both eternity and impermanence.
Among the four calculations, the first holds that the Buddha is neither eternal nor impermanent.
Next, regarding the four propositions concerning the lifespan of the Buddha:
one follower of the Hīnayāna calculates that the Buddha's lifespan ends with a single lifetime and is therefore finite.
Second, the Mahāyāna school maintains that the Buddha’s lifespan is eternally infinite.
Third, with respect to the three bodies (trikāya), it is both finite and infinite.
Fourth, according to the Middle Way, it is neither finite nor infinite.
These constitute the twelve types.
Having fully refuted these twelve types of Buddha, the Master of the Treatise [concludes that] the opponent claims that there is no Buddha at all.
This constitutes the thirteenth [point].
Furthermore, to refute the view that everything is utterly non-existent, yet ultimately claim that the Buddha exists and is ineffable,
constitutes the fourteenth.
This treatise refutes fourteen types of false Buddhas and establishes the True Buddha;
therefore, it is titled "The Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata.
Question: For what reason are these fourteen kinds of Buddhas refuted?
Answer: It is refuted for three reasons.
First, because those [positions] mutually contradict one another, they refute themselves.
Second, the Buddha is not the fourfold propositions (catuṣkoṭi), and the fourfold propositions are not the Buddha.
It is not that the Buddha was defeated because he was merely a Buddha;
rather, the Buddha possesses both essence and function,
and his function is such that his transformative teachings are boundless and manifold.
Regarding the four propositions, if one follows the nature of the entity itself, it is neither four nor not-four.
Those [opponents] do not recognize its function; within their own applications, each clings to a single extreme.
For this reason, they are refuted.
Furthermore, another master of the Three Treatises (Sanlun) says:
"In this context, there are two interpretations regarding the refutation of the Tathāgata.
The first states:"
It is merely that one’s attachment to the mind is what is destroyed; in reality, the Buddha is not destroyed.
Second, it is said:
even if the Buddha were destroyed, it would be only the Buddhas of the non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna who are destroyed.
Now, it is clear that this is not so.
If merely destroying the mind of attachment were called "destroying the Buddha," then they would ultimately maintain that the Buddha exists, but simply do not permit attachment to him.
Investigating the fourfold erroneous attachments regarding the meaning of the Tathāgata in this chapter is of vital importance.
Nowadays, students do not reflect upon these profound mysteries and thus lack faith;
however, if they read them with a careful mind and direct their attention toward them, there will be great benefit from their deep engagement.
Therefore, regarding the contemplation of the Tathāgata:
those of both the Great and Small Vehicles who encounter or meet a Buddha say they see the Buddha;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is said that the Buddha is not seen.
That is to say, the Buddha is one who possesses right view,
whereas the non-Buddhists are those with false views who make such distinctions;
neither of them truly knows the Buddha.
Now, this chapter exhorts one to observe well: what is the Buddha,
and what is not the Buddha?
Nowadays, people all say,
"I am a disciple of the Buddha;
having served the Buddha, I now teach and transform others."
If one does not discern with precision whether a person is a Buddha or not a Buddha, or who is truly a disciple and who is the one they serve,
this chapter is required for that purpose.
It enables those studying the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna to gain a true understanding of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

For the most part, they do not find peace in this place.

If one refutes the Tathāgata in this manner, the third section below analyzes why neither emptiness nor existence is the Buddha.
"The Tathāgata transcends conceptual proliferation" concludes the fourth section, which rebukes the externalist opponents.

the first [chapter] refutes this existence.

when the outsider hears that there is something which is not the Buddha,
he then claims that emptiness must be the Buddha.
Therefore, next is the refutation of emptiness.

how, then, can it be called the Buddha?

An outsider asks: [Why is this so?]
If both emptiness and existence were not the Buddha, then there would be no Buddha at all;

both persons and phenomena are empty.
To rebuke outsiders who erroneously claim [the existence of] persons and dharmas,
there are two general reasons why one first refutes the person and subsequently refutes the dharma.
First, because "Buddha" is a personal name, the person is refuted first.
Having finished refuting persons by means of persons, one now adheres to the dharma as being the Buddha;
therefore, next, the dharma is refuted.
Second, there is the sequence of difficulty and ease regarding the two types of emptiness: the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of dharmas.
Because the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) is easy to realize, the person is refuted first;
because the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is difficult to realize, phenomena are refuted later.
Within the refutation of the person, four gates are opened.
First, the section clarifying that the Buddha and the aggregates are neither identical nor different.
Next, the second section, asking: "In this sense, [the Buddha] is neither self-produced nor produced by another in relation to the aggregates.
Finally, the third section, beginning with: "If [the Buddha] does not depend on the five aggregates, [he is] neither prior nor posterior to the aggregates."
If, within the discussion of identity and difference, one concludes at the fourth level that the Buddha cannot be apprehended,
these four gates can universally refute the attachments of both internal and external, as well as Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna schools.

third, he refutes the Buddha of the Mahāyāna.

this refers to the sequence of shallow and deep.

Question: Now that you are refuting the Buddha, why do you employ the fivefold search (*pañcavidha-paryeṣaṇā*) for your refutation?
Answer: This is the opponent’s formal statement establishing his position:
"The Buddha is an omniscient person.

one now returns to seeking the Buddha through those same five ways.

if you say there is no Buddha, you fall into false view."
The master of the treatise avoids the extremes of existence and non-existence,
yet captures two points from the opponent:

"Why is this? introduces the second explanation. This explanation states that there are two faults in [the view that] the aggregates (skandhas) exist:
first, since the aggregates are subject to arising and ceasing, the Buddha would also be subject to arising and ceasing.

who would maintain its merit and wisdom?

the three types of supernormal knowledge cannot know it,
as explained in the "Chapter on the Five Aggregates."

Question: If that is so, the "Adornment" (Mahāvyutpatti) clarifies that the Buddha does not encompass existence or non-existence;
how does this differ from the present text?
The answer has already refuted the notion that [the object] is neither existent nor non-existent;
therefore, one should not ask this question again.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
To maintain that things are neither existent nor non-existent is the discourse of the deluded;
how could one who is deluded be considered a Buddha?
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
The Buddha and his disciples know that apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no further phenomenon.
If one were to emerge outside of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), such a person would be neither a Buddha nor a disciple.
This interpretation is produced by a mind of false conceptualization.

Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* and this treatise clarify that the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and nirvāṇa are synonymous terms.
How, then, can it be said that the Buddha emerges outside of nirvāṇa, or that the Buddha emerges outside of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
The second half correctly rebukes outsiders who, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, differentiate between existence and non-existence.
It asks: why do those deluded ones differentiate between existence and non-existence after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata?
Answer: Because sentient beings perceive that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa and that there is no longer a Buddha, they engage in various forms of repudiation.
The followers of the Hīnayāna say:
The Buddha’s physical body has been extinguished and his wisdom is identical to the great void;
therefore, there is no Buddha.
Thus say the followers of the Mahāyāna.
The Dharma-body is eternally abiding;
for this reason, there is a Buddha.
This initial point is also the doctrine of the Sthavira school.
The following is established by the *Saṃghabhedavastu*.
In the fourth chapter, "Reproving Outsiders," which follows the refutation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is stated:
"If one says that the Buddha is subsumed within the two truths, or that he stands outside the two truths."
All such things as these are mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

Regarding those who have been reborn in the higher realms, it was previously explained that whether the Tathāgata is in the world or has passed into extinction, he is neither existent nor non-existent.
Yet, deluded persons engage in conceptual proliferation, reckoning him as either existent or non-existent.
The latter half refutes the fallacies of existence and non-existence.
Master Xinghuang said:
"To cling to the Tathāgata as definitely existing or as impermanent or non-impermanent [is an error]."
It surpasses the five heinous crimes by destroying the Dharma-body.
The long prose section states:
"This is the fifth chapter, arising from within the 'Tathāgata' section."
It reveals the marks of the Tathāgata;
as for what is called "beginning, middle, and end," at the beginning of this chapter, the refutation of existence is the Tathāgata,
and in the middle, the refutation of the four positions such as emptiness is the Tathāgata.
The subsequent analysis demonstrates that the Tathāgata is neither entirely non-existent nor definitively existent;
this concludes the three preceding chapters.
The fourth section merely serves as a reprimand.
It is not concluded because it does not constitute a separate refutation.
The verse consists of two parts:
the first half indicates the nature of the Tathāgata, and the second half explains the first half.
The understanding that the nature of the Tathāgata is identical to the nature of the world is explained through three meanings for which this statement was made.
First, at the beginning of the chapter on "Non-Buddhists" (Bāhyaka), the supramundane was cited as proof for the existence of the mundane.
The Master of the Treatise now cites the mundane to illustrate the supramundane.
Since the four positions of existence and non-existence regarding the mundane cannot be found,
the same applies by extension to the supramundane Tathāgata.
Second, when the outsiders hear that the aforementioned refutation of the four positions regarding existence and non-existence shows them all to be non-Buddhist,
they claim that the Buddha transcends these four positions and dwells beyond the hundred negations.
Therefore, it is now clarified that the nature of the Tathāgata is itself the nature of the world.
It is not only when a Buddha appears that the four propositions transcend the hundred negations.
The world is likewise so.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says:
"Contemplate the true reality of the body."
Contemplating the Buddha is likewise so.
Third, this arises from the reprimand in the fourth chapter.
Since the preceding verse already stated that the Tathāgata transcends conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), [the present verse follows].
The outsider then claims that conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) itself is the mundane,
whereas the Tathāgata is supramundane; thus, they give rise to the dualistic view of the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
Therefore, it is now clarified that the nature of the Tathāgata is itself the nature of the world;
it is not merely that the Tathāgata transcends the four propositions.
These four phrases are, from the very beginning, not four; they are themselves the Tathāgata.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Lust itself is the Way."
The same applies to hatred and delusion.
The second half [of the verse] explains the first half,
clarifying that the Tathāgata, like the world, transcends the four propositions.
Therefore, the two natures have no distinct nature;
that which has no distinct nature is the essence (*tattva*).
Chapter 23: Contemplation of Perversions (end of section 9). Chapter Twenty-three: Contemplation of Perversions. Question: Four chapters have refuted supramundane dharmas.
Why, then, does it refute the inverted views?
The answer is: while the previous section did not fail to refute supramundane views, it primarily refuted mundane ones.
Later, it primarily refutes the supramundane.
Second, because one wishes to manifest the non-duality of the mundane and the supramundane,
one refutes the mundane within the context of the supramundane.
Third, it further reveals that to conceptualize the existence of supramundane phenomena is itself an inversion;
therefore, to refute supramundane dharmas is called "refuting inversions.
Fourth, for those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) to conceptualize the body of the Tathāgata as suffering and impermanent is termed an inversion.
Since one has given rise to inverted views regarding the supramundane Dharma,
one must therefore eliminate those inversions within the supramundane.
Fifth, the body of the Tathāgata is in reality neither existent nor non-existent, yet one calculates it as being either existent or non-existent.
This is precisely what constitutes perversion;
therefore, we now refute this perversion.
For those of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles, there are only two dharmas.
First is the mundane,
and second is the supramundane.
Having finished refuting the mundane in the preceding section, the supramundane is now raised as a remedy.
Having now finished refuting the supramundane, [the author] returns to cite the mundane to provide a remedy.
Because those whose minds are characterized by external acquisition cannot remain without some point of reliance or attachment,
the two positions are alternately cited and established in sequence.
Question: Since the chapter on the defiled has already refuted the afflictions (*kleśa*), this is equivalent to refuting the inversions (*viparyāsa*).
Why, then, are they refuted again?
Answer: Afflictions are difficult to refute.
Therefore, it is necessary to refute many [positions].
Furthermore, the previous refutation of defilement was a refutation of craving;
the present refutation of perversion is a refutation of views.
Because all sentient beings do not transcend craving and views.
Question: For what reason does [the text] refute the Tathāgata first, and subsequently refute the inversions?
Answer: Speaking from the perspective of those who are deluded, there are generally two meanings.
First, regarding one's own practice:
the Tathāgata is the person who is able to abandon [defilements],
while inversion is the delusion that is to be abandoned.
Regarding the transformation of others, the former [case] is like the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world,
while the latter is for the purpose of severing the afflictions of sentient beings;
therefore, the former refutes the Tathāgata.
Next, the refutation of misconceptions:
Second, if this arises from the preceding text, the end of the "Superior" section states:
"That which is the nature of the Tathāgata is itself the nature of the world."
The outsider said:
"The world takes afflictions as its nature;
the Tathāgata takes freedom from defilement as his essence."
Why, then, say that the Tathāgata is the nature of the world?
Therefore, it is now clarified:
the non-arising of inversion is itself the Tathāgata.
Question: What constitutes inversion?
Answer: Inversions are both general and specific.
As for the general, everything that involves apprehension of objects is inversion.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Sentient beings, due to the conditions of inversion, wander through the six realms of existence.
To speak of them specifically, there are three inversions, four inversions, twelve inversions, and eight inversions."
The three inversions refer to perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*).
The Abhidharma states that perception and mind are not the essential nature of inversion.
However, because they are disturbed by perversion, they are called "perversion.
The Vibhajyavādins say that all three are the essence of perversion.
The Satyasiddhi masters offer two interpretations.
One says: when consciousness is deluded regarding reality, it is called a "perverse mind" (citta-viparyāsa).
The delusion of the aggregate of perception regarding the provisional is called the perversion of perception.
When the mind within the aggregate of formations is deluded by the former two perversions, it constitutes the perversion of view.
Second, it says:
Judging from the perspective of their single essence, the mind itself is determined to be the substance of the three perversions.
When the essence is distorted, it constitutes the perversion of mind;
when divergent perceptions arise therefrom, they constitute the perversion of perception.
Perversion through erroneous determination constitutes a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭiviparyāsa*).
Among these three perversions, those of heavy grade belong to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while those of light grade belong to the afflictions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
The inferior grade belongs to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Now, according to Nāgārjuna’s intention, all that possesses mind is a perversion of mind;
whatever involves conceptualization is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
Whatever is perceived is entirely a perverted perception (*viparyāsa*).
Question: Regarding the arising of the three perversions and the severing of the two [perversions], how are they similar or different?
Answer: As explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun), in the commentary on the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*).
This clarifies that the three inversions differ in their time of arising and differ in their time of abandonment.
At the time of arising, first the inversion of perception and mind arises, followed by the inversion of view;
this proceeds from the lighter to the heavier.
At the time of abandonment, views are abandoned first, while perception and mind are abandoned later;

therefore, the perversion of view belongs to that which is abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya), whereas perception and mind belong to that which is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya).
The four inversions refer to conceiving of saṃsāra as permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Question: What constitutes the essence of these four inversions?
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* answers:
"Its essence consists of the mental factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃskāra*).
Question: Among the five views (*pañca-dṛṣṭi*), how many are inversions (*viparyāsa*) and how many are not inversions?
The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* answers:
"Two and a half views are perversions.
Within the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), there is both the self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*)."
To view the self as "I" is a perversion;
to view what belongs to the self as "not-I" is not a perversion.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
The combination of "I" and "mine" is termed the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*).
Among the extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), there is both nihilism and eternalism;
taking the view of permanence as permanent constitutes the inversion of permanence (*śāśvata-viparyāsa*).
Among the types of adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), there is that which is independent and complete;
the estimation of what is not pleasant or pure as being pleasant and pure is this independent adherence to views.
This is called the inversion of pleasure and purity.
As for the other two and a half views,
they refer to the grasping at views within the category of false views and the extreme views that involve the delusion of nihilism.
This is not an inversion. Question: Why is this so?
Answer: Only when five conditions are fulfilled is something designated as an inversion.
First, it refers to those whose nature is dull and indolent.
Second, it arises conditioned by the truth;
that is to say, it is an affliction of delusion regarding principle.
This briefly clarifies the delusions regarding phenomena.
Third, "arising above the fruits" means arising upon the Truth of Suffering.
Fourth, "the correct inversion of characteristics."
Beneath the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) lies the principle of suffering and impermanence.
Now, as we are precisely overturning the Truth of Suffering,
one instead conceives of permanence, bliss, and self.
Fifth, it is independent and not located upon the feet.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* further states:
"It is called 'inverted' because it possesses three characteristics."
First, the nature of intensity;
second, false apprehension;
third, inversion of sameness.
The view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is of a violent nature but is not a perversion, because it destroys its object;
likewise, attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is of a violent nature and is a false grasping, yet it is not a perversion of the same kind [as other perversions].
The remaining two and a half views possess all three characteristics. In the *Abhidharmakośa*, the three characteristics are established as "perversions" (*viparyāsa*):
first, because they increase what does not exist, such as conceiving a self where there is no self.
Second is determination;
third is turning away from objects, which is easy to understand.
These two views and a half possess these three meanings.
The remaining two and a half views do not increase existence.
Next, the twelve inversions are explained as taught by the Sthavira school and the Vibhajyavādins.
Within each of the four inversions, there are perception, thought, and view;
therefore, they are called twelve.
Eight are abandoned through the vision of the truths, and four are abandoned through the path of cultivation.

The eight [misconceptions] abandoned through the path of vision are as follows: regarding the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception; regarding the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of view.
The same applies to the remaining three.
Therefore, these eight belong to those abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*).
As for the four belonging to those abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), they consist of the four types of inverted minds.
When one reaches the stage of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), all eight inversions are completely severed.
This reaches the point where the four [inversions] are severed at the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*).
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* cites another master who states:
"Among the twelve types [of inversions], the four types of inverted views belong to those abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*)."
The eight [afflictions] belong to what is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Some teachers say:
"Only the view is the inversion."
There are only four [types of] inversions, not twelve.
Furthermore, they are abandoned only by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and not by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*);
they are afflictions belonging only to the level of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), not those belonging to the levels of the other three truths.

Question: Since those who have attained the first and second fruits of the path are free from the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), how can they give rise to defiled attachment and still engage in the rites of husband and wife?
Answer: The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* provides two explanations.
One explanation states that there are two ways in which the notions of pleasure and purity arise: first,
they arise with respect to the principle of the Truths (*satya*).
For those who have attained the first two fruits, it does not exist;
for those who give rise to it within the realm of phenomena, it does exist.
Next, the commentary explains:
When those who have attained the first or second fruits of the path give rise to defiled attachment,
they actually do conceive the perception of impurity and suffering; however, they do so out of necessity,
like the analogy of the Brahmin who forged his finger.
Who would know that the finger was impure?
It was only because of the pain that he placed his fleshy finger in his mouth;
this case is just like that.
Regarding the twelve inversions (*dvādaśa-viparyāsa*), the Vibhajyavādins state that the three— namely,
the inversions of perception (*saṃjñā*), mind (*citta*), and view (*dṛṣṭi*)— are the basis.
Each of these gives rise to the four [inversions] of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, thereby forming the twelve inversions.
If one follows the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*, it is said that only when the mind arises accompanied by mental factors (*caitta*) is it termed a "perversion" (*viparyāsa*),
as previously explained.
Regarding what are called the eight inversions, the masters of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* maintain that they consist of the perceptions (*saṃjñā*),
thoughts (*citta*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*) that give rise only to the four inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*),
but do not give rise to the [opposite] four— suffering, impermanence, non-self, and impurity— pertaining to the subsequent stage of Buddhahood.
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* say:
"The eight inversions [of the four truths] in their preceding and succeeding stages are all afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*),
not afflictions of deliberation (*vicāra-kleśa*)."
Among the views, three belong to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
the inversion of self belongs to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and the inversion of permanence belongs to the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
The [notions of] pleasure and purity belong to the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
To claim that what is impermanent is permanent, or that what exists is non-existent,
is subsumed under false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the latter four inversions are subsumed under ignorance (*avidyā*).
The reason for this is that persons of the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Since the latter four inversions still arise even then,
we know that they are subsumed under ignorance (*avidyā*).
This interpretation should be accepted.
Question: Previously, ordinary beings who were non-Buddhists within the cycle of birth and death conceived the four inversions, such as permanence;
whereas those of the Two Vehicles further gave rise to the four [inversions] regarding the Dharma-body, such as impermanence.
Regarding the statement that there are eight inversions when discussing both ordinary beings and sages together:
can it be said that those of the Two Vehicles also possess all eight inversions at present?
Answer: They indeed possess them all.
Because they reckon the Buddha-ground to be impermanent, there are the four [perverted views] such as impermanence;
furthermore, they cling to their own nirvana as being permanent and blissful—
this is precisely the misapprehension of the impermanent as permanent.
The reason for this is that the nirvana of the two vehicles is in reality impermanent and without bliss, yet they reckon it as permanent and blissful; therefore,
they possess the four inversions, such as the inversion of permanence.
Question: Since those of the two vehicles do not conceive of *nirvāṇa* as a self, how can they possess the inversion of regarding what is not-self as self?
Answer: There are two kinds of "self."
The self of persons and the self of phenomena:
although there is no grasping at a self of persons, the existence of nirvāṇa is itself the self of phenomena.
Therefore, there is the inversion of self.
It is easy to understand that ordinary persons possess all eight inversions.
This chapter fully refutes both the general and specific inversions.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Refuting Perversions.
Question: How does this chapter refute both general and specific perversions?
Answer: Within this chapter, it refutes not only the eight perversions.
Furthermore, this also refutes the eight modes of the opponent's position; thus,
one should know that reckoning birth and death as either permanent or impermanent is entirely a perversion.
Even the four lines are all inversions;
this is the refutation of general inversions.
Specifically refuting the four inversions and so forth is the refutation of particular inversions.
Question: How does one destroy inversion?
Answer: Both those within and without, as well as those of the Great and Small Vehicles, all claim that things exist; this is inversion.
They do not know that the intrinsic nature of inversion is empty and quiescent.
Now, when one seeks this inversion, it cannot be found;
this is itself the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Destroying Inversion."
Furthermore, both those within and without, as well as those of great and small capacity, all say that there is the arising of inversion;
yet when they seek to extinguish it, the inversion is not extinguished.
Now, one seeks the inversion and finds that it is fundamentally unarisen from the beginning.
Now, since it is also not extinguished,
the inversion is thereby extinguished;
hence it is called "the destruction of inversion."
Furthermore, when outsiders perceive the two characteristics of the inverted and the non-inverted, they—being ignorant—assert that there are two:
namely, clarity and ignorance. If they calculate [the existence of] these two, the inverted and the non-inverted, [they fall into error].
Then both the inverted and the non-inverted would both become inverted.
Now, realizing that the inverted and the non-inverted are fundamentally without two distinct characteristics,
then both the inverted and the non-inverted are termed "non-inverted."
Therefore, this [section] refutes such inversions.
Regarding the various divergent interpretations of this chapter, most do not reach the essential point.
Now, it shall be divided into two parts.
The first [section] refutes the meaning of the arising of afflictions through inversion;
the second refutes the meaning of the extinction of afflictions through inversion, provided that the nature of afflictions were real.
The reason for opening these two [sections] is that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as both Buddhist and non-Buddhist schools, speak in this way.
Previously there arose the afflictions of inversion, and subsequently the path of cultivation was practiced to sever them and bring about their extinction;
for this reason, it is now clarified.
Afflictions are fundamentally non-arising;
they do not cease even now.
Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
Subhūti, if you do not sever the afflictions,
yet do not dwell together with them, then you may accept this food.
To dwell together with the afflictions refers to ordinary worldlings.
The severing of afflictions refers to the Two Vehicles.
Now, in the first chapter, by seeking the arising of afflictions and finding it impossible, the meaning of their non-coexistence is explained.
In the subsequent chapter, by demonstrating that afflictions do not cease, the meaning of their non-severance is clarified.
The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions teach the dharma of repentance,
yet they do not sever the ocean of fetters and afflictions."
Not dwelling in the ocean of fetters is likewise the same as this;
these two chapters constitute the Vaipulya Great Repentance.
In every thought-moment, one is able to see Samantabhadra and the Buddhas of the ten directions, whereby heavy karmic offenses are extinguished.
Furthermore, these two chapters show that observing the non-arising and non-ceasing of perversions is itself the Middle Way, giving rise to right contemplation.
Furthermore, one contemplates that non-arising and non-extinction are themselves the Dharma-body and Nirvana.
Thus, the *Wuxing jing* says:
"The three poisons are the path of immeasurable Buddhas."
The first chapter is further divided into two parts.

The first part, "First, the prior refutation of afflictions and inversions," concludes with the phrase "Thus, these inversions are extinguished. The second part, "The concluding summary refuting the underlying intention," follows below that.
One who resolves to break through conceptual thought can thus engage in the correct contemplation of this chapter;
thereby, afflictions and inversions will be ultimately and eternally extinguished.
Any contemplation other than this is a false contemplation.
Not only are the former delusions not eliminated,
but new inversions arise once more.
Regarding the first [of these], there are again two [aspects].
First one destroys afflictions, and next one destroys perversions.
The reason for destroying these two is that by destroying afflictions,
one destroys those sentient beings who, being householders, give rise to craving.
To destroy perversions is to destroy the views of those who have left the household life and those external paths;
furthermore, it is to destroy the afflictions arising from celestial Māras and the perversions arising from external paths.
Furthermore, afflictions arise from those of dull faculties,
while inversions arise from sentient beings of sharp faculties;
moreover, afflictions arise from ordinary worldlings.
The followers of the Two Vehicles give rise to inverted views.
Question: Why is it that afflictions are refuted first and inverted views are refuted later?
Answer: Previously there were householders who gave rise to craving;
subsequently there were renunciants who gave rise to views.
Therefore, within the burning house, the venomous insects are explained first.
Regarding the subsequent discussion of evil spirits:
those who wish to emerge from the burning house should rely on this chapter to observe them.
Furthermore, according to the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there are generally four types of persons.
The first are those of dull faculties who give rise to craving;
they do not know weariness with saṃsāra, nor do they know how to escape from it.
Second, the heterodox practitioners who possess inverted views;
they know weariness with the world but do not know the way out.
Third, those of the Two Vehicles.
Knowing weariness and knowing emergence—
these are merely indirect ways of emerging.
These are the four types of bodhisattvas.
Based on this chapter, one correctly contemplates reality as it is, thereby knowing weariness with cyclic existence and knowing the way out;
this is called "direct emergence.
Regarding the first [section], the destruction of afflictions is further divided into four distinct parts.
First, establishment; second, refutation; third, rescue; fourth, refutation of the rescue.
"Conceptualization and discrimination" refers to the establishment of the causes of the three poisons.
"Arising" refers to the production of the effects of the three poisons born from greed, anger, and delusion.
Regarding the inversion of purity and impurity: this explains how results arise from causes.
By means of the inversion of purity and impurity, the three poisons are produced;
that these all arise from causes and conditions clarifies the mutual production of two kinds of phenomena.
First, they arise from the inversion produced by recollective thought and discrimination;
second, the three poisons arise from the inversions of purity and impurity.
Therefore, it is said that all things arise from a multitude of conditions.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says:
"Desire has inversion as its root;
inversion has conceptualization and discrimination as its root."
The conceptualization of discrimination takes non-abiding as its basis.
The five verses in the response constitute five distinct sections.
1. Refutation by means of the gate of the initial absence of intrinsic nature;
2. Refutation by analogy of the person to phenomena;
3. Refutation by the absence of belonging.

The fourth and fifth [arguments] seek to refute [the opponent's position] by means of cause and effect. The first two [arguments] are as follows: 1. Refutation by means of the cause. 2. Refutation by means of the effect. 3. Refutation by seeking to break [the opponent's position]. 4. Refutation by using the cause to illustrate the effect. 5. Refutation by using the cause to illustrate the effect. The first two [arguments] are as follows: [list omitted].
The first half restates [the opponent's position] and the second half refutes it:
If afflictions possessed an intrinsic nature, they could not arise from causes;
if they arise from causes, they lack intrinsic nature.
If afflictions were of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), they would be empty;
however, the sūtras clarify that afflictions arise from causes and conditions.
Consequently, the opponent claims that afflictions do exist.
The Master of the Treatise states the intent of the Sūtra:
that which arises from causes and conditions is itself emptiness.

Therefore, next, the refutation of their cessation is presented in two verses.
First, it is refuted that afflictions possessing an intrinsic nature can be extinguished.
Second, when one deconstructs afflictions as mere designations, there is nothing to be extinguished.
All afflictions do not transcend the conventional nature of designation.
Furthermore, the initial deconstruction of afflictions demonstrates that they belong to the person and are thus shown to be unextinguishable.
Next, when destroying afflictions, there is no person to whom they belong,
nor can they be extinguished.
Furthermore, at the outset, it was clarified that the afflictions of those who follow the Hīnayāna cannot be extinguished.
Next, the refutation of the afflictions of the Mahāyāna demonstrates that there is nothing to be extinguished.
In each case, the first half of the verse restates the opponent's position and the second half provides the refutation;
the text is easy to understand.

Question: If that is so, the Sūtra states that the wisdom associated with a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇasamprayuktā prajñā*) severs the afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
How can you now say there is no severance?
Answer: If one says there is something to be severed, then the afflictions are not severed.
Now, in this context, since that which is sought to be severed cannot be found, the afflictions are thereby severed.
Furthermore, one sees that afflictions are cultivated and severed by the Path;
it is not merely that the afflictions themselves are not severed,
for upon those afflictions, there further arise the maladies of subject and object.
This means that there is the remedial path which acts as the agent of abandonment,
and the afflictions which are the objects to be abandoned;
now, upon realizing that the nature of the afflictions is empty, both of these "diseases" are simultaneously stilled.
The Commentary on the Madhyamaka-śāstra, Scroll Nine, End.
